title: A wedding song at a funeral
word: A wedding song at a funeral
hook: Sohila is also sung at cremations, a song of the soul going home

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was now is the time, and the trader's question: what did I earn today? This is a week's end too: the sky's aarti, the wind, the city of thieves, Guru Arjan's request. Today, where else Sohila is sung. Day four hundred thirty-four.
screen: `NOW IS THE TIME.` · `A WEEK: THE AARTI, THE CITY, THE REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Most traditions keep their wedding music and their funeral music far apart. You don't play the first dance at a graveside. But a Sikh family standing at a cremation will hear something that sounds, if you know the words, like it belongs at a wedding: friends at the door, the date written, oil poured at the threshold, blessings for the bride. It's Sohila, the same five hymns many of them said in bed last night. And nobody there thinks it's out of place.
screen: `WEDDING MUSIC, FUNERAL MUSIC.` → `AT THE CREMATION: SOHILA.` → `THE SAME FIVE HYMNS AS LAST NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, sets out the funeral. The body is washed and dressed, and the family gathers. At the cremation ground, once the pyre is lit, the sangat recites Kirtan Sohila, and then the Ardas is said. Afterward there is often a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib in the days that follow. Sikh teaching also asks mourners not to give way to loud wailing. Grief is real, and tears are human, but the songs are of praise. So why Sohila, of all hymns? Go back to day one of the first hymn. The date has been written. Friends, pour the oil, give your blessings, so I may meet my Lord. The summons goes to every house, every day. For many Sikhs, the funeral is the day that summons arrives for one soul, and the wedding in the hymn is the meeting with the Beloved. The person they loved isn't being lost to darkness. In the language of the hymn, they're going home, the way a bride goes to her new home. Notice what that does to the night. If the same five hymns are sung at bedtime and at the end of a life, then every night is a small rehearsal. You lie down, let go of the day, and trust the morning to the One. And the last line of Sohila, sung at the pyre as well as at the pillow, is Guru Arjan asking to be the dust of the holy's feet. Even at the end, humility.
screen: `THE PYRE IS LIT; SOHILA IS SUNG.` · `PRAISE INSTEAD OF WAILING.` · `THE SUMMONS ARRIVES FOR ONE SOUL.` · `EVERY NIGHT, A SMALL REHEARSAL.` · then, large: `GOING HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think kindly of someone who died. Let one person come to mind: a grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, maybe someone you barely knew but remember. Picture their face as it was on a good day. Remember one thing they did well, one kindness, one habit, one laugh. If grief comes up, let it come; nothing needs fixing. Hold them in your mind like a friend at the door wishing a traveler well. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them, softly. The bell holds the time.
A wedding song at a funeral. Kirtan Sohila, sung at Sikh cremations as well as at bedtime: the soul as a bride, called to meet the Beloved and going home.
screen: `A WEDDING SONG AT A FUNERAL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: going home. Tonight, as you lie down, let the day go the way the hymn lets a life go: with praise, and with trust. Day four hundred thirty-four.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sohila, a song of praise and joy; sung at bedtime and at the cremation ground.

trapdoor: what you thought: it's strange to sing about a wedding at a funeral.
what it means: in Sohila the soul is the bride and the wedding is the meeting with God, so the song fits the day a soul goes home.
what a scholar hears: the Sikh Rehat Maryada prescribes Kirtan Sohila and Ardas at the cremation, and discourages wailing; sohila was also a name for festive songs.

notes: Rehat Maryada funeral order: Kirtan Sohila recited when the pyre is fully lit, followed by Ardas; a sahaj or akhand path afterward is common; mourners asked not to wail. Confirm details and wording.
